sites.name: Grand Egyptian Museum
sites.hook: The biggest archaeological museum in the world, built for one civilisation and placed about 2 km from the pyramids.

story.title: The colossus that moved house twice
story.text: The giant Ramesses II in the atrium was found in pieces near Memphis in 1854. In 1955 it was raised in a Cairo square, in front of the main railway station, and pigeons and traffic circled it for fifty years. In 2006 it was lifted out and trucked to Giza, and in 2018 it moved again, into the museum's atrium, before the building was even open. The statue is about 11 m tall and weighs around 83 tonnes. Tomorrow you will meet its smaller, fallen cousin at Memphis, where it was found.

steps: Entrance plaza: the hanging obelisk of Ramesses II
Grand Atrium: the colossus of Ramesses II
Grand Staircase: statues lined up in time order
Top of the stairs: window onto the pyramids
Galleries: tombs, temples, daily life
Tutankhamun galleries: the whole tomb in one place
Khufu's boat, if on your route (ask)

dont_miss.d: About 10 kg of solid gold. Look at the eyes (quartz and obsidian) and the vulture and cobra on the brow.
Dozens of statues of kings, queens and gods. Walk up slowly and read the labels: you are climbing through time.
From the top of the Grand Staircase a glass wall frames the Giza pyramids. A good moment for the family photo.

dont_miss.t: The dagger made from a meteorite
dont_miss.d: Among Tutankhamun's objects is an iron blade. Iron was rarer than gold then. Analysis showed it came from space.
Carter found it crammed into four small rooms. Here the objects are spread out, so you can see how many there are: over 5,000.

easy: Turn the mask around in your mind: a protective spell is written across its shoulders.
Tutankhamun's own childhood things (a stool, small objects) sit among the grand ones. They make him a kid.
Look for broken noses on statues. Many were damaged on purpose, to 'switch off' the statue.
The museum is built on the desert plateau edge: look outside the glass at the sand-coloured stone.
ask: Which objects here were found exactly where Carter photographed them, and which were moved?
How do we know the dagger is meteoritic iron, and how did it get to Egypt?
Why were so many statues' faces damaged, and by whom?
What is in these halls that the old museum in Tahrir Square could not show?
How do you decide what goes in a case and what stays in a storeroom?
quests: Look closer
Find one object made of a material that does not come from Egypt (lapis lazuli, cedar, ebony, turquoise, obsidian). Where did it come from? What does that say about trade?
Estimate
The mask weighs about 10 kg. What else weighs about that? How many gold masks fit in a backpack, and why would that be a terrible idea?
tips: It is large and tiring. Ask the guide for the highlights route and agree a toilet stop before the Tutankhamun galleries.
Rules on photography and bags vary and change. Ask at the entrance before you take anything out.
Eat and drink before you go in. Prices inside are museum prices.

sites.name: Dahshur, the two Sneferu pyramids
sites.kicker: Day 2 afternoon · south of Giza · replaces the Citadel, the mosque and the souk
sites.hook: One pyramid that went wrong and one that worked, built by the same king. Almost nobody is there.
facts: about 40 km south of Giza, roughly 1 h by road

story.title: Sneferu's problem
story.text: Sneferu was the father of Khufu. His builders had already seen the Step Pyramid, and he wanted smooth sides. At the Bent Pyramid they began at a steep angle of about 54 degrees. Halfway up, with the walls cracking inside, the angle was cut to about 43 degrees. The result is the bent shape. Next to it they tried again at the gentler angle from the start. That is the Red Pyramid, the first true smooth-sided pyramid. Everything at Giza rests on these two experiments.

steps: Arrive at the Bent Pyramid: walk the base
Look up: the top still wears its smooth casing
Drive or walk to the Red Pyramid
Climb the entrance stairs, if you want to go in
Down the long passage to the first chamber
Up the corbelled vault to the second chamber
Back outside: compare the two slopes

dont_miss.d: It keeps more of its original polished limestone skin than any other big pyramid. This is how Giza once looked.
Stand back far enough to see the bend. It is the most honest piece of engineering history in Egypt.
A steep stair, a low passage, then chambers with stone roofs shaped like upside-down staircases. Take a torch.
No queues. You hear the wind. This is what the plateaus were like before the crowds.

easy: The Red Pyramid is named for the reddish tint of its stone, best at sunset.
Look at the stone courses: they tilt inward, a trick that made the Red Pyramid stable.
A small satellite pyramid stands near the Bent Pyramid.
Far across the desert, the mud-brick lump of another pyramid is visible from here (the Black Pyramid, much later).
ask: Do we know why the angle changed: a collapse, cracks, or a decision to finish faster?
Why did Sneferu build more than one pyramid?
How do we date these pyramids, and what do the quarry marks tell us?
Is the interior open today, and how long is the passage?
quests: Look closer
Photograph the Bent Pyramid from three distances. At which distance does the bend become obvious?
Estimate
The Red Pyramid is about 104 m tall. How many floors of a typical building is that? Compare it with the tallest building you know.
tips: The inner passage of the Red Pyramid is steep, hot and low. Skip it without guilt if anyone dislikes small spaces.
Closed shoes, hats and water. There is almost no shade.

This replaces the Citadel, the Mohamed Ali mosque and the Khan el-Khalili souk of the printed programme. Suggestion: confirm the change with the Sakkara Tours representative on arrival, since their driver and timing decide it.

sites.name: Memphis
sites.kicker: Day 3 morning · Mit Rahina, in a palm grove
sites.hook: The capital of Egypt for centuries, now a garden with a few statues. It teaches how a city can vanish.
facts: The fallen colossus and the alabaster sphinx

story.title: Where did Memphis go?
story.text: For over a thousand years, Memphis was the place where Egypt was run. The Greeks heard the name of its great temple of Ptah, Hut-ka-Ptah, as 'Aigyptos' and gave the whole country its name from it. Then the city faded, and its stones went into new buildings, many of them in medieval Cairo. One of the largest ancient capitals in the world became a field of palm trees, and then a car park for a museum. What you see is a handful of survivors.

steps: Garden entrance and palm grove
The fallen colossus of Ramesses II, seen from a gallery
The alabaster sphinx
Stelae and smaller statues in the garden
The alabaster embalming table, if signposted

dont_miss.d: It is limestone, about 10 m long, found in 1820. Compare it with the granite one you saw yesterday at the Grand Egyptian Museum.
Smooth, pale and over 3,000 years old. It is usually attributed to a New Kingdom king, and the face is deliberately idealised.
Stand in the middle and ask yourself where the temple of Ptah, the god of builders, once stood.

easy: A huge alabaster table with lion-shaped sides was used to embalm Apis bulls, sacred animals of Memphis.
Count the cartouches on the colossus. A name in an oval rope is a king's name.
The ground here is still rich farmland. The river has moved east over the centuries, uncovering and burying things.
ask: Where was the ancient city, and where would the palaces have been?
Why did we lose Memphis but keep Giza?
What was the Apis bull, and where was it buried?
How do archaeologists search for a city under farmland?
quests: Look closer
Find a cartouche. How many signs are inside, and can the guide read it aloud?
Debate
If a future generation found only your school's front gate, what would they conclude about your town?
tips: A short stop. Shade is rare and ticket-booth souvenirs are cheap. Say 'La, shukran' with a smile if you do not want anything.

sites.name: Saqqara
sites.kicker: Day 3 · the Step Pyramid of Djoser
sites.hook: The first large stone building in history. Everything you will see later started here.
facts: Imhotep, the first one we know by name

story.title: A pyramid by trial and error
story.text: Before Djoser, kings were buried under flat mud-brick benches called mastabas. His architect Imhotep built one in stone, then added a smaller one on top, and another, and another, until it rose in six steps to about 60 m. Imhotep was remembered for centuries as a genius and eventually worshipped as a god of healing. The Greeks later identified him with their own healing god. The pyramid is a pile of experiments, which makes it the best place to understand the idea.

steps: Imhotep Museum, if time allows (ask)
Entrance colonnade, a covered corridor of stone columns
Great South Court
The Step Pyramid up close
The Heb-Sed court with its dummy chapels
The serdab, the sealed room with peepholes
Optional: Unas causeway or a decorated mastaba (ask)

dont_miss.d: Ribbed stone columns that copy bundles of reeds. People were learning to build in stone by copying what they knew in plants and wood.
The enclosure wall had 15 gates. Only one is real. The rest are carved stone.
A small stone box with two holes. The king's statue sat inside to look out and receive offerings. The one here is a copy.
Solid stone buildings that look like shrines. They were made for the king's afterlife and cannot be entered.
The wall alone was about 10 m high and over 1.6 km long. Look at what is left.

easy: Inside the Heb-Sed court, look for the B-shaped marker stones that outline the ritual running track.
Notice the tiny stones used for walls: they are small blocks, like bricks, because stone building was new.
The nearby pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BC) is the first with writing inside. The interior is usually closed.
Mastabas such as Mereruka and Ti have the best everyday reliefs: boats, farming, animals. Ask if one is possible.
ask: How do we know Imhotep designed it, and what else do we know about him?
Why six steps and not five or seven?
What is under the pyramid? How long are the tunnels?
Why a false door, and who was fooled?
Which mastaba would you visit if you had one hour?
quests: Look closer
Find a stone column that looks like a bundle of reeds. Draw it, then draw what you think the original building was made of.
Estimate
Djoser's pyramid is about 60 m, Khufu's was about 147 m. How many Djosers fit on top of each other to reach Khufu?
tips: Sand, rubble and bright light. Wear sunglasses and closed shoes.
Interiors of pyramids and tombs are not promised in your programme. Ask the guide what is open that day.

sites.name: Giza and the Sphinx
sites.hook: The last of the seven wonders of the ancient world still standing. Photos hide the scale.
facts: Khufu: about 147 m originally, 138 m today

story.title: Who built it? Merer wrote it down
story.text: For years people said slaves built the pyramids. Then in 2013, archaeologists at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea found papyri with the logbook of a foreman called Merer. In it, he and a team of about 40 men move limestone by boat along the Nile to Giza, for Khufu's pyramid, and he notes the days they spent on each trip. They were paid, organised in crews with names, and fed. Nearby at Giza, their bakeries and cemetery have been found. The Great Pyramid was built by Egyptians who knew exactly what they were doing.

steps: Panorama point: all three pyramids together
Khufu: walk to the base and touch a block
Khafre: look for the casing still on its top
Menkaure: the smallest, with a gash in its side
The Sphinx and the temple at its feet
The valley temple of Khafre with its granite pillars (ask)

dont_miss.t: A single block at Khufu's base
dont_miss.d: Each block weighs about 2.5 tonnes on average. There are over two million. Stand next to one.
Near the top of Khafre's pyramid you can still see the smooth limestone skin that once covered all of them.
About 73 m long and carved out of the rock of the plateau itself. Walk around it to see its body.
Between the Sphinx's paws is a stone telling how prince Thutmose IV fell asleep in its shadow and dreamed that if he cleared the sand, he would become king.
Khufu is the biggest, Menkaure the smallest. Khafre looks the biggest because it stands on higher ground.

easy: The Sphinx's missing nose was not shot by Napoleon's army. Drawings from 1737 already show it missing.
Look at the north face of Menkaure's pyramid: a vertical gash. In 1196, a ruler tried to dismantle it, gave up after months, and left the scar.
Small queens' pyramids stand beside each big one. Count them.
The workers' town and cemetery lie south of the Sphinx. They are excavation sites, usually closed, but you can look in their direction.
ask: What did the workers eat, and where did they sleep?
Where did the stone come from, and how was it brought?
What did the Sphinx look like when it was painted?
What did the ScanPyramids team find inside Khufu's pyramid in 2017?
Where was Khufu's boat found, and where is it now?
quests: Look closer
Find three differences between Khufu's and Khafre's pyramids (angle, casing, setting, size).
Estimate
Khufu's pyramid has about 2.3 million blocks. If a block was set every two minutes, working 10 hours a day, how many years would that take? What does that tell you about the size of the workforce?
tips: Camels, horses and photographers will approach. A clear 'La, shukran' is enough. Agree any price before you start.
The Great Pyramid's interior is not part of your programme. The diagram shows what is inside.
A Sound and Light show is available separately (60 EUR per person, in French, as listed in your programme).

sites.name: The Nile days and the Esna lock
sites.hook: Long sailing days are the best way to understand Egypt: a green strip between two deserts.
facts: Day 5 about 3 h, Day 6 about 5 h, Day 8 about 7 h, Day 9 about 4 h
Esna, built by British engineers in the early 1900s

story.title: Wind north, current south
story.text: The Nile flows north. The wind blows mostly from the north. So a boat can sail upstream with its sail up, and float downstream with its sail down. The Egyptians noticed, and their hieroglyph for 'south' is a boat with a sail, and for 'north' a boat without one. Egypt's whole geography is in that pair of signs. At Esna, the river is held back by a barrage and boats wait their turn in the lock, often for hours. Small trading boats tie up beside the cruise ships, and the sellers throw their goods up to the decks.

steps: Day 5: leave Luxor, sail about 3 h to Esna
Esna lock: a wait, then the gates
Evening: moor near Edfu
Day 8: long sail back (about 7 h), past Kom Ombo
Day 9: Edfu to Luxor via the Esna lock

dont_miss.d: Look for the exact line where irrigated fields stop and desert begins. On this bank, you could stand with one foot on each.
A real piece of engineering you will wait inside. Watch the gate open and close.
Water buffalo, farmers in galabeyas, children waving, sugar cane, palm groves, small boats.
Egrets, herons, kingfishers and hoopoes. The sun deck at dusk is the best seat.

easy: Look for the shaduf, a pole with a bucket and counterweight, used to lift water for thousands of years.
Some village houses in Upper Egypt are painted with scenes of the pilgrimage to Mecca. It is a local tradition.
The ancient Egyptians had three seasons: flood, growing, harvest. The dam ended the flood.
At dusk, the temples are lit up. Watch the shoreline as you pass.
ask: How high did the river used to rise before the dam?
What crops grow along this bank?
How does the lock work, and who runs it?
Why do you have so many boats on the Nile?
quests: Look closer
Make a deck list of ten things you see in one hour: a bird, a boat type, a crop, a house colour, an animal. Compare lists at dinner.
Estimate
On Day 8 the boat sails about 7 hours from Aswan towards Edfu, roughly 110 km by river. What is its average speed in km/h? Does the current help or slow it?
tips: Take a hat and a long-sleeved shirt for the sun deck. The breeze hides the sun.
Cabins, pool and sun deck are the family's time to rest. Plan one slow hour on each sailing day.
Wi-Fi on board is paid, in common areas only (about 9 to 11 EUR per day in your programme). Download the guide before you board.

sites.name: Luxor Temple
sites.hook: A temple in the middle of a modern city, with a working mosque on top of it.
facts: Amenhotep III (c. 1390 BC), Ramesses II (c. 1250 BC)
The place where the god Amun came to visit, once a year

story.title: The obelisk that lives in Paris
story.text: Two obelisks once stood at this gate. In 1829 Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali offered one to France. It was lowered onto a purpose-built ship, sailed down the Nile and across the Mediterranean, and in 1836 it was raised in the Place de la Concorde, where it stands today. The other one stayed here. When you see the single obelisk at Luxor, you are looking at the twin of one you may have walked past in Paris. Each year, in the flood season, the statue of Amun was carried here from Karnak, along the avenue or on the river, for a festival called Opet.

steps: The Avenue of Sphinxes and the pylon: obelisk and colossi
Court of Ramesses II (the angled one)
Colonnade of Amenhotep III: the tall papyrus columns
Sun Court and the inner halls
The Roman painted chamber and the shrine of Alexander (ask)
Up above: the Abu el-Haggag mosque on the court

dont_miss.t: The obelisk and the seated colossi
dont_miss.d: The pylon is 24 m high and shows Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh. His name is cut on almost everything.
Fourteen columns shaped like papyrus buds, each about 19 m tall. They line the road that the god's procession followed.
Abu el-Haggag has stood here for about 800 years. Egypt's layers (temple, church, mosque) are all in one view.
Scenes along the colonnade show the procession: boats, priests, music. A film storyboard in stone.

easy: The court of Ramesses II is askew compared with the rest of the temple. He angled it to line up with older shrines.
In the Roman chamber, a painted ceiling covers the old reliefs. Soldiers once used this room.
Count the seated colossi at the pylon and the standing ones in the court. Some are missing.
Each year the Abu el-Haggag festival carries boats through the streets, a living echo of Opet.
ask: What happened in this temple at the Opet festival, day by day?
Why was the court built crooked?
How was the obelisk moved to Paris, and how did Egypt feel about it?
How can a mosque stand on a temple without damaging it?
Where does the Avenue of Sphinxes start, and can we see a piece of it?
quests: Look closer
Find the Battle of Kadesh on the pylon. How do you tell Ramesses II from his soldiers? Think about size, position and what each one is doing.
Debate
Should France keep the Paris obelisk? Make the case in two sentences each, one for keeping it and one for returning it.
tips: Morning light is gentle, and the temple is calm. Read the colonnade scenes at a slow pace.
Evenings, the temple is lit up. If you have the energy on another evening, ask the boat's reception.

deep.guide_line: One walk from the sphinxes to Alexander's shrine, in the order the god's procession used the temple, with the right light for every photo.

briefing.intro: Luxor Temple is long and narrow, about 260 metres from gate to back wall, and runs roughly north to south, parallel to the Nile. The river and the corniche are on its west side, the town and the mosque square on its east side. The gate faces north-northeast, towards Karnak, because this temple was the end of a road: once a year the god Amun travelled here for the Opet festival. Everything is arranged for that arrival: an avenue, a gate, an open court, a corridor of columns, a second court, a hall, and small dark rooms where only the king and the priests went. We walk it the way the god did, north to south, and the building gets older, lower and darker as we go. Romans, Christians, Alexander the Great and a Sufi saint have all left marks on the way. About an hour with me, then half an hour on your own.

know.d: It was dedicated to Amun, Mut and their son Khonsu, but its real subject seems to be the king. The Chicago Epigraphic Survey reads it as a temple of the royal ka, the king's divine double. At Opet the king met the god here and came out renewed, confirmed for another year.

Amenhotep III built most of it from the colonnade southwards, around 1390 BC. Ramesses II added the gate and the first court around 1250 BC. In between, Tutankhamun decorated the colonnade and Horemheb cut his own name over Tutankhamun's. The names on the walls change as you walk.

The front part is turned several degrees against the back part. Ramesses II angled his court and gate, probably to face the road to Karnak and to keep an older shrine of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III standing on the spot. Scholars still argue about which reason mattered most.

By the nineteenth century the temple lay under a hill of sand, rubble and houses about fifteen metres high. Gaston Maspero began clearing it in 1884 and the work went on until the 1960s. The mosque on top was never removed, so its door now hangs high above the temple floor.

Reliefs run in rows called registers, read in the direction the figures face. Sunk relief, cut into the surface, works outside where hard sun makes deep shadows; raised relief, standing proud, was used indoors.

Around AD 300 the Romans built a legionary fortress around the temple and turned one hall into a shrine for the emperors. Christians later built churches in and around it, and in the thirteenth century a mosque rose on the buried court. Every layer is still visible. The Opet story itself is in episode s06.

In the morning the sun comes in low from the east-southeast, over the town and the mosque. It lights the west side of each court and the inner face of the west walls, and throws column shadows towards the river. Afternoon is the reverse.

numbers: about 25 m; its Paris twin about 23 m
Statues once in front of the pylon
Statues found under the Sun Court in 1989

tour.title: The Avenue of Sphinxes
tour.where: North of the temple, on the paved avenue. Stand between the sphinxes and face south-southwest, towards the gate.
tour.look: Two rows of human-headed sphinxes on lion bodies line the road. Most carry the name of Nectanebo I, about 2,400 years ago, a thousand years after Amenhotep III. Behind you the road runs 2.7 kilometres to Karnak. Just before the gate, in the western part of the paved square, are the low brick walls of a Roman chapel to Serapis and Isis, dedicated in AD 126 on the emperor Hadrian's birthday.
tour.story: This was the arrival lane. The procession came down here with the god's boat on the priests' shoulders, stopping at way stations to rest. The sphinxes were crowd barrier and guard of honour at once: a lion's body for strength, a king's face for authority. The avenue disappeared under houses and fields; excavation began in the mid-twentieth century and the whole road reopened with a night parade in November 2021. From here you see the temple as designed, head on, the gate filling the sky.
spot: Nectanebo's cartouche on a sphinx base
The Roman chapel's brick walls

tour.title: The pylon and the Battle of Kadesh
tour.where: About 30 m from the gate, on the axis, facing the two towers.
tour.look: A pylon is a ceremonial gateway of two sloping towers. This one, by Ramesses II, is about 24 metres high and 65 wide. The four tall grooves held cedar flagpoles with pennants. The sunk reliefs show his campaign against the Hittites at Kadesh, in Syria, in his fifth year: the army camp, the surprise attack, and the king in his chariot shooting into a tangle of enemies. Morning sun rakes in from the east and lifts the carving.
tour.story: Kadesh, around 1274 BC, was close to a draw. The Egyptians were ambushed, one division was routed, and Ramesses fought his way out until reinforcements arrived. He then had it carved as a personal triumph on at least five temples. Years later Egypt and the Hittites signed one of the oldest peace treaties whose text survives. This wall is propaganda: a giant king, tiny enemies, no near-disaster.
spot: The four flagpole grooves
The king in his chariot, twice anyone's size
tour.ask: Which tower shows the camp and which the battle?

tour.title: The obelisk and the colossi
tour.where: Still in front of the pylon. Facing the gate, the obelisk is on the east side, your left.
tour.look: One piece of pink Aswan granite, about 25 metres high, covered in Ramesses II's titles. On its base, baboons raise their arms to greet the rising sun. The partner stood on the west side; the empty plinth is where it was. Two granite colossi of the king sit before the towers, about 14 to 15 metres high, and four standing statues once joined them. Count how many stand today. One black granite colossus, found in 1958 in 57 pieces, was put back on its feet in 2017.
tour.story: Around 1830 Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali gave the western obelisk to France. A purpose-built ship took it down the Nile and across the sea, and it was raised in the Place de la Concorde on 25 October 1836, its baboons sent to the Louvre. The two obelisks were never the same height: the shorter one stood a little forward on a taller base, so from the avenue they looked equal.
spot: The baboons on the base
The empty western plinth
Small queens standing by the king's legs

tour.title: The Court of Ramesses II
tour.where: Through the gate, stop just inside. You face south-southwest; west is on your right.
tour.look: An open court about 57 by 50 metres, ringed by 74 columns in a double row with closed papyrus-bud capitals. Colossi of the king stand between the southern columns. On your right, in the northwest corner, a small triple shrine with red granite columns: a resting place for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu, built by Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. Now look to the far end. The colonnade is not quite in line with the gate behind you.
tour.story: Ramesses kept the old shrine, wrapped his court around it and turned the new front a few degrees towards Karnak. He also reused older statues: about five of the court's eleven standing colossi were made for Amenhotep III and recut with Ramesses' names. On the south wall, west of the colonnade entrance, look for a carved picture of this very temple front, with flags, obelisks and statues, and a line of royal sons bringing offerings. Ramesses had more than a hundred children.
spot: The triple shrine in the northwest corner
The carved picture of the pylon
Recut cartouches on a colossus

tour.title: The Mosque of Abu el-Haggag
tour.where: The east side of the court, on your left as you face south. The mosque sits on the northeast corner.
tour.look: A white mosque with a brick minaret, standing on the rubble that once filled the court, its floor many metres above the stone pavement you stand on. On the court side, find a doorway high in the wall, opening onto nothing: the mosque's entrance when the court was still buried. Ancient columns of the court are half swallowed in its walls and still carry the building.
tour.story: Yusuf Abu el-Haggag was a Sufi holy man, born around 1150, said to have come from Damascus by way of Mecca, who settled in Luxor and died here around 1245. The mosque over his tomb dates from the thirteenth century, with later rebuilding and a restoration in the 2000s. When the temple was cleared, the town kept its mosque. His yearly festival carries boats through the streets, which many link to the Opet barques. The link cannot be proven; the shared place is real.
spot: The door hanging above the temple floor
Columns swallowed by the mosque wall
tour.photo: In the morning it is backlit from the court: shoot it as a silhouette, or from the southwest corner.

tour.title: The colonnade and the Opet reliefs
tour.where: Walk between the two seated colossi at the south end of the court into the corridor of tall columns.
tour.look: Fourteen columns in two rows of seven, about 16 to 19 metres high, with open papyrus-flower capitals. It was roofed and walled; only the lower walls survive, and on them is the Opet procession. The west wall, on your right as you walk south, tells the outward journey: the boats leave Karnak, are towed up the river and reach Luxor. The east wall shows the return. In the morning the west wall is in raking sun and the east wall in soft shade.
tour.story: Amenhotep III began this as the nave of a hall he never finished. Tutankhamun had it decorated, and the carving was incomplete when he died young. Horemheb then cut his own name over Tutankhamun's, and Seti I finished the southern end decades later. It is one of the few places where you can stand in front of large work commissioned by Tutankhamun. Find the barges hauled on ropes, the soldiers, the musicians and the acrobats bent over backwards.
spot: Acrobats doing back-bends
Teams hauling the barges
A cartouche where Horemheb replaced Tutankhamun

tour.title: The Sun Court and the hypostyle
tour.where: At the south end of the colonnade the space opens into an older court. Stop in the middle, then walk on into the columned hall.
tour.look: The peristyle court of Amenhotep III, around 1390 BC, the best preserved part of his temple. Double rows of papyrus-bundle columns with closed-bud capitals run along three sides, the stone warmer and the carving finer than Ramesses' work. Count the stems in a bundle and the bands that tie them. Beyond it is the hypostyle, a hall of 32 columns in four rows of eight, once roofed and dim, the floor rising towards the sanctuary.
tour.story: In January 1989 workers checking the court's foundations found statues about a metre under the floor. In the end 26 came out, from the New Kingdom to the Ptolemies, including a superb quartzite Amenhotep III, now in the Luxor Museum. Priests buried them carefully, perhaps to retire old statues, perhaps to hide them in troubled times. Nobody knows for sure. The hall beyond is the threshold: each step in is darker and more private, and at Opet the god's boat disappeared into it out of the sun.
spot: The bands tying each papyrus bundle
The floor rising in the hall

tour.title: The Roman chamber
tour.where: Go through the south end of the hypostyle into the room behind. The old central doorway is now a curved niche.
tour.look: This was an offering hall of Amenhotep III. Around AD 300, under Diocletian and the four co-emperors of the Tetrarchy, the Romans blocked the doorway to the sanctuary with a curved apse and plastered over the Egyptian reliefs. On the plaster they painted the emperors on the south wall, and officials, soldiers and horses moving towards them on the side walls. Where the plaster has fallen, Amenhotep's carving shows through underneath.
tour.story: The temple had become the core of a Roman legionary fortress, and this room a shrine where soldiers honoured the emperors and their standards. The traveller John Gardner Wilkinson copied the paintings in the nineteenth century, then they faded under grime. American and Egyptian conservators cleaned them over three seasons in the 2000s and found far more colour than expected: rare imperial Roman wall paintings, still in place, inside a pharaoh's temple.
spot: Pharaonic relief under Roman plaster
Soldiers' legs and horses' hooves
An emperor's foot on a jewelled stool

tour.title: Alexander's shrine and the birth room
tour.where: Walk around the apse into the dark rooms south of it. The small shrine stands in the middle of a chamber.
tour.look: Inside Amenhotep III's barque room stands a smaller shrine built in the name of Alexander the Great, around 330 BC. On its walls Alexander, dressed as pharaoh, offers to Amun, sometimes in his fertility form, Amun-Min. His name is in hieroglyphs in a cartouche. The sanctuary where Amun's statue stood is behind. In the birth room on the east side, the god Khnum shapes the baby Amenhotep III on a potter's wheel.
tour.story: Alexander took Egypt in 332 BC and was welcomed as the man who drove out the Persians. At the oracle of Amun in the western desert he was hailed as the god's son. A shrine here, in the room where kings renewed their power, said the same thing in stone: I am pharaoh too. He probably never came to Luxor. The Greek dynasty that followed him, the Ptolemies, played the same role for three centuries.
spot: Alexander's cartouche
Khnum at his potter's wheel

alone.intro: This is where I leave you. The temple is one straight line with one exit at the north end, so you cannot get lost: south is deeper in, north is the way out. Four ways to use the next half hour.

plans.d: Walk back north through the hypostyle and the Sun Court. In the colonnade, read the west wall slowly from south to north for the barges, musicians and acrobats. In the first court, find the carved picture of the pylon on the south wall, then stand under the mosque's hanging door. Finish at the obelisk and its baboons.

Stay five minutes in the Roman chamber while your eyes adjust to the frescoes, then look into the birth room. Check the Sun Court columns for paint. Read both colonnade walls, west first. Walk around the triple shrine, then leave by the avenue and go 100 metres north between the sphinxes for the front view.

Morning shade sits on the west side of each court, under the column rows. Move north along those west colonnades and sit on the low walls. Drink before you are thirsty. The younger ones can do the statue census from the shade.

alone.meet: Meet in front of the obelisk at the north end, the one landmark everybody can find. Add five minutes for the photo someone will insist on.

photos.where: On the Avenue of Sphinxes, 25 to 35 m north of the pylon, on the axis.
photos.when: Early morning, sun low in the east-southeast, lighting faces from the side.
photos.how: Family in a line between two sphinxes, tallest at the ends. Crouch at hip height, 0.5x, so obelisk and towers rise over the heads. Tap a face to expose.
photos.avoid: The gateway itself, where the queue funnels strangers into the frame.

photos.where: East of the axis, by the obelisk base, the east tower behind.
photos.when: Morning, while the tower has raking light.
photos.how: One person a step from the base, photographer kneeling three metres away at 1x to keep the obelisk straight.
photos.avoid: Cutting off the tip; guards' chairs at the base.

photos.where: Southwest corner of the Court of Ramesses II, looking northeast.
photos.when: Mid-morning, sun side-on from the right.
photos.how: Chest height, 0.5x, horizon level: columns left, gate centre, mosque top right, one small person for scale.
photos.avoid: Shooting the mosque from the west early: the sun sits right behind it.

photos.where: North end of the colonnade, looking south along the east row.
photos.when: Morning, column shadows across the floor.
photos.how: Stand by the first east column at 0.5x and let the row run out of frame. Family at the base of the third column, tiny.
photos.avoid: The middle of the aisle at 1x: flat and full of groups.

photos.where: West wall of the colonnade, lower register.
photos.when: Morning, when sun rakes across the relief.
photos.how: Shoot at an angle along the wall, 2x, so the raking light shows the carving.
photos.avoid: Afternoon, when this wall falls into shade and flattens.

photos.where: West colonnade of the Sun Court.
photos.how: Two or three people between columns, faces in open shade, bright court behind. Expose on the faces.

photos.where: Corniche promenade on the west side, looking east over the railings.
photos.when: Late afternoon or dusk, sun behind you over the west bank; backlit in the morning.
photos.how: Family at the railing, temple below and behind. Phone raised to clear the railing; night mode at dusk.
photos.avoid: Lamp posts and wires at the top of the frame.

photos.where: Front square, 20 to 30 m from a seated colossus.
photos.how: One person holds out a flat hand; line the statue up to sit on it. Shoot low at 1x.

details.d: Baboons chatter at sunrise, so Egyptians made them the sun's greeters. The Paris obelisk's baboons are in the Louvre.
The four slots in the pylon held cedar masts taller than the towers. They are drawn on the carved picture of the pylon inside the court.
The mosque's old door, high on the court wall, marks the ground level of medieval Luxor, many metres above the pharaohs' floor.
South wall of the Ramesses court, west of the colonnade: the temple front with pylon, flags, obelisks and colossi, as it looked when new.
Several colossi in the first court were carved for Amenhotep III and recut for Ramesses II. Look for cartouches with uneven, deeper outlines.
In the colonnade, Horemheb's cartouches cover Tutankhamun's. Ask your guide for one where the older signs still show.
Early Christians carved small crosses and built churches in and around the temple. Ask your guide to show you a trace.
Ramesses II's front is greyer and coarser, Amenhotep III's work warmer and finer. The change shows at the colonnade.
Travellers have scratched names here for centuries. Please do not add one: a tourist's graffito in 2013 made world news.
In the front square, low brick walls of a Roman chapel to Serapis and Isis, dedicated in AD 126 on Hadrian's birthday.

qa.a: Ramesses II turned his new court and gate a few degrees off Amenhotep III's axis. The usual reasons: to face the road to Karnak, the whole point of the building, and to keep the older triple shrine of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. Some add the line of the riverbank. It was deliberate; how much each reason weighed is still debated.

Ordinary people reached the avenue and perhaps the front court on festival days. The colonnade and courts beyond were for priests and officials, the sanctuary for the king and highest priests only. At Opet the crowd watched the shrine arrive and vanish inside.

qa.q: Why is Ramesses II's name everywhere?
qa.a: He reigned about 66 years and was Egypt's busiest builder. He added the front of this temple and cut his name onto older walls and statues. For a king, a name on a monument joined him to it forever and showed that he kept the gods' houses in order. Reusing older works was common; Ramesses did it on a grand scale.

qa.q: How did the obelisk get to Paris?
qa.a: French engineers built a flat-bottomed ship, the Luxor, able to sail on the Nile and at sea. They lowered the obelisk in 1831 with ropes and a timber cradle, floated it down to the Mediterranean and on to France, and raised it in the Place de la Concorde on 25 October 1836 before a huge crowd.

qa.q: What was buried under the Sun Court?
qa.a: In 1989 workers found a pit of statues about a metre down: 26 in the end, from Amenhotep III to the Ptolemies, many in excellent condition, now in the Luxor Museum. Priests buried them deliberately and carefully. Whether to clear space, to retire statues no longer used, or to hide them in a dangerous moment, nobody can say for sure.

qa.q: Why did the Romans paint over Egyptian reliefs?
qa.a: Around AD 300 the temple was inside a Roman military camp, and this hall became a shrine for the four co-ruling emperors. The Romans plastered the walls to get a flat surface to paint on; to them the reliefs were just walls. The plaster partly protected the carving beneath, and the paintings are among the best surviving Roman imperial frescoes.

qa.q: Did Alexander the Great come here?
qa.a: Probably not. He was in Egypt in 332 to 331 BC, founded Alexandria and visited Amun's oracle at Siwa, but there is no good evidence he reached Thebes. The shrine was built in his name during his reign by Egyptian priests and craftsmen, to show him as a legitimate pharaoh in the most royal room of this temple.

qa.q: How can a mosque sit on a temple?
qa.a: When it was built in the thirteenth century, the court was buried. The mosque stood on the rubble, with walls resting on ancient columns. When the temple was dug out from the 1880s, the rubble around it went but the mosque stayed, carried by what lay beneath.

practical: Plan about 1.5 hours: an hour guided, then 20 to 30 minutes alone.
Morning is best: soft light, fewer groups, shade on the west side of each court.
Little shade in the front square and first court: hats, sun cream, a full bottle each.
Closed shoes: uneven paving, steps and door sills between halls.
Phones are normally fine. No flash on painted walls; check rules for tripods on the day.
Do not climb on statues or walls, and do not touch the Roman frescoes.
Hawkers wait at the exit and on the corniche: a firm 'la, shukran' (no, thank you) and keep walking.
Day 5 is long: Karnak follows, then sailing. Save the younger ones' energy and eat a snack in between.

kids.d: Six statues of Ramesses once stood before the pylon. How many stand today?
On the west colonnade wall find someone bending over backwards, someone making music and a team pulling a rope. First to find all three picks dessert.
In the shade by the obelisk, draw one baboon from the base in two minutes.
Stand in the first court on the line from gate to colonnade and find where it bends. Teenagers: estimate the angle in degrees, then ask the guide.
Should the mosque be moved to restore the temple, or stay as part of its history? Two minutes a side, parents judge.
Learn sunk relief versus raised relief, then test the adults on three walls. They must explain why sunk relief is used outside.

glossary.d: King around 1390 to 1352 BC, builder of most of the temple.
King around 1279 to 1213 BC; added the pylon, obelisks and first court.
The yearly festival of Amun's visit from Karnak.
A monumental gateway of two sloping towers.
A model boat carrying a god's shrine on poles.
A hall whose roof rests on many columns.
Thirteenth-century Sufi saint whose mosque stands on the temple.

tonight: Who would you have been in the Opet procession: hauler, musician, acrobat or priest?
Ramesses II put his name on other kings' statues. Stealing, or looking after them?
Should the Paris obelisk come back to Luxor?

sites.name: Karnak
sites.hook: The biggest religious complex humans ever built. Thirty kings added to it over about 2,000 years.
facts: from about 1950 BC to Roman times

story.title: The hall of giants
story.text: Step into the Great Hypostyle Hall. 134 stone columns stand in 16 rows. The twelve down the middle are about 21 m tall and their tops open like papyrus flowers. The side columns are shorter, so a band of windows at the top lets in a stripe of light. Seti I began the hall and his son Ramesses II finished it, about 3,300 years ago. It was once roofed and painted in bright colours. You are walking through a forest of stone plants, designed to feel like the first marsh at the beginning of the world.

steps: Avenue of ram-headed sphinxes
First Pylon, then the Great Court
The Kiosk of Taharqa: one column left
Great Hypostyle Hall
The obelisks of Hatshepsut and Thutmose I
Sacred Lake and the giant scarab
Festival Hall of Thutmose III (if time)

dont_miss.d: The ram is Amun's animal. Between the paws of each one is a tiny statue of a king.
Stand in the middle row and look up. Notice the windows and the leftover paint on the architraves.
About 30 m of one piece of red granite from Aswan, the tallest still standing in Egypt. The tip was once covered in gold.
Priests washed here before ceremonies. Locals say seven laps around it bring luck. Ask the guide what it promises.
A granite beetle on a pedestal beside the lake, a symbol of the sun's rebirth.

easy: On the First Pylon's back face, look for a long ramp of mud brick, thought to be a leftover construction ramp.
A long inscription at Karnak records the peace treaty that Ramesses II made with the Hittites. Ask the guide where it is.
The Hypostyle Hall's outer walls carry battle scenes of Seti I and Ramesses II.
Thutmose III walled in Hatshepsut's obelisks. Look for traces of where the wall stood.
Look for old graffiti: travellers have scratched their names into Karnak since Greek and Roman times.
ask: Which king built which part? Can you show us the oldest piece?
How was the roof placed on 21 m columns?
Why was the Great Court's pylon never finished?
What did priests do here every day?
What is the Treaty of Kadesh, and where is it on the wall?
quests: Look closer
Find three ways a column can be decorated: papyrus, lotus, carved figures. Which is which?
Estimate
The tall columns in the hall are about 21 m high. If a person is 1.7 m, how many people stacked up reach the top?
tips: Go early or late: better light, fewer crowds. Little shade, so hat, water and sun cream.
Sound and Light is optional (60 EUR per person, in French, per your programme).

deep.guide_line: Two hours through the largest temple complex of ancient Egypt in the order the god's procession used it, with the right spot and light for every photo, then half an hour on your own.

briefing.intro: Karnak is a city of temples. The main precinct, the house of Amun-Ra, covers about 25 hectares inside a mud-brick wall, and some thirty kings added to it over two thousand years. The main axis runs roughly east to west, tilted a little: the front gate faces west-northwest, towards the Nile, and the sanctuary lies about 400 metres in, towards the east-southeast. We walk it the way the god's boat did, from the river end inwards: rams, the unfinished gate, the Great Court, the Hall of Giants, two obelisks, the sanctuary, Thutmose III's festival hall. Rule of thumb: the further east you go, the older the stone. We end at the Sacred Lake, where I leave you for half an hour. The hall's story is in s07, Ramesses II's battle in l03.

know.d: Pylons are numbered in the order you meet them, almost the reverse of the order they were built. The First Pylon, at the front, is about 2,350 years old. The oldest temple, Senusret I's, around 1950 BC, stood behind the sanctuary and is now an empty court with a few granite thresholds.

Amun-Ra is the hidden god of Thebes fused with the sun god Ra. He lived here with his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, the moon god. Mut has her own precinct to the south, Khonsu a smaller temple in this one's south-west corner. Ordinary people rarely came past the outer courts.

In raised relief the background is cut away and figures stand proud: delicate, best in soft light. In sunk relief the figure is cut into the wall, with deep edges that read in hard sun and are harder to erase. The Hypostyle Hall has both: Seti I's raised work in the north half, Ramesses II's sunk work in the south.

In late October the sun rises in the east-southeast, behind the sanctuary, and sets in the west-southwest, over the river. In the morning the front of the First Pylon is backlit; in the afternoon it is lit. At midday the sun is high in the south. North-facing walls get no direct sun this month.

Kings filled new pylons with older buildings. Inside the Second, Ninth and Tenth Pylons, archaeologists found tens of thousands of small talatat blocks from Akhenaten's sun temples; inside the Third Pylon, whole chapels of Senusret I and Hatshepsut, now rebuilt in the Open Air Museum.
Six pylons line the main east-west axis. Four more, the Seventh to the Tenth, run south towards the temple of Mut and the road to Luxor Temple. Ask your guide what is open today.
Expect scaffolding. A Franco-Egyptian team has worked here since 1967, and recent cleaning in the Hypostyle Hall has brought back reds, blues and yellows high on beams and capitals.

numbers: about 113 m wide, 15 m thick, unfinished
nearly 30 m, over 300 tonnes, one stone

tour.title: The quay and the avenue of rams
tour.where: Walk from the visitor centre to the forecourt and face east-southeast, towards the huge gate.
tour.look: Two rows of lions with rams' heads lead to the doorway. The ram is Amun's animal. Between the front paws of each stands a small mummy-shaped king, protected by the god. Behind you, the raised platform at the west end of the forecourt is an ancient quay, where the god's river barge moored when the Nile or a canal reached this far.
tour.story: Most of these rams carry the name of the high priest Pinedjem, who ruled Thebes as a near-king about 1050 BC and reused older statues. More rams stood further in; when the Great Court was built they were moved to its sides. This was the god's river door.
spot: The little king between a ram's paws
The quay platform behind you
A ram with a restored head
tour.photo: Morning: shoot across the row, not at the backlit gate. Afternoon: shoot down the row to the lit gate.

tour.title: The First Pylon and the builders' ramp
tour.where: Walk through the doorway, then turn round inside the court to see the back of the south tower.
tour.look: Outside, the stone is rough and uncarved except near the door: the gate was never finished, and the north tower stops lower than the south one. Inside, a big slope of mud brick leans against the back of the south tower. It is a builders' ramp, left where the work stopped. High in the doorway, nineteenth-century travellers carved their names.
tour.story: The pylon is usually dated to Nectanebo I, about 2,350 years ago, of the last native dynasty before the Persians returned in 343 BC. Work stopped and never resumed. The ramp, a grid of brick walls packed with rubble, is rare physical evidence of how blocks went up layer by layer.
spot: The mud-brick ramp
Travellers' names high in the doorway
tour.ask: How high was the pylon meant to go, and which names in the doorway are the oldest?

tour.title: The Great Court: Taharqa's column and Seti II's chapel
tour.where: Just inside the gate. The lone column is in the middle of the court; Seti II's small chapel is in the north-west corner, close on your left.
tour.look: The court is about 100 by 80 metres. The single column, about 21 metres, is the last of ten from the giant open kiosk of Taharqa, around 680 BC. At its foot is an alabaster block where the god's boat was set down. Seti II's chapel has three small rooms side by side, for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu. Rams sit in rows along the court's sides.
tour.story: Taharqa came from Kush, in today's Sudan, and ruled Egypt for about 26 years before the Assyrians pushed him south. His kiosk had no stone roof: it was a stone copy of a light shelter of poles and matting, where the procession paused.
spot: The alabaster boat stand
Three doors of Seti II's chapel
Rams moved to the side of the court
tour.photo: Family in one line at the column's foot, phone low and six metres back, 0.5x vertical.

tour.title: The temple of Ramesses III and the Bubastite Portal
tour.where: Cross to the south side of the court. The small complete temple cuts through the colonnade, its gate facing north.
tour.look: A whole temple in miniature: a little pylon, a court lined with statues of the king as Osiris, arms crossed, a columned hall and three sanctuaries. To its east, in the court's south-east corner, a gateway leads out: the Bubastite Portal.
tour.story: Ramesses III built this about 1180 BC as a rest stop for Amun's boat, outside the temple of his day. On the outer wall beyond the Bubastite Portal, Shoshenq I lists towns he took in Palestine around 925 BC, each name in an oval fort topped by a bound captive. Many scholars identify him with Shishak, who the Bible says raided Jerusalem; others doubt the match.
spot: Osiris statues with crossed arms
Shoshenq's town list outside the portal
tour.ask: Can we step through the Bubastite Portal to see Shoshenq's list?

tour.title: The Second Pylon and the colossus
tour.where: East end of the court, at the doorway in the half-ruined gate. The colossus stands beside it.
tour.look: The broken tower shows its inside: rough fill, not solid masonry. The granite colossus, about 15 metres with its base, is Ramesses II with a small princess against his legs, usually identified as his daughter Bentanta. The high priest Pinedjem later added his own name.
tour.story: Horemheb began this pylon about 1300 BC and packed its towers with blocks from Akhenaten's demolished sun temples, showing Akhenaten, Nefertiti and their daughters under the sun's rays. The pylon's back face is the west wall of the Hypostyle Hall.
spot: The princess at the colossus's feet
Exposed fill in the broken tower
tour.photo: One person beside the colossus's base gives the scale. Keep out of the doorway crowd.

tour.title: The Hypostyle Hall: the central aisle
tour.where: Step through the Second Pylon, walk ten metres down the central aisle and stop between the first pair of giant columns.
tour.look: Twelve giant columns with open papyrus capitals line the aisle; 122 shorter columns with closed buds fill the wings. Look up: above the shorter columns, on both sides of the nave, are the tall clerestory windows. A few still hold their stone grilles. On the underside of the beams, find blue, red and yellow paint.
tour.story: The story of the hall is in s07; here is how to use it. Walk to the crossing, where the north-south aisle meets the central one, about two thirds of the way in, and look down four avenues of columns. From mid-morning to early afternoon the sun, high in the south, drops bright patches through the southern windows and roof gaps onto the nave and the northern wing.
spot: A surviving stone window grille
Paint on the beams
The crossing of the two aisles
tour.photo: Phone almost on the floor at the base of a giant column, 0.5x, straight up the shaft.

tour.title: The north wing and Seti I's battle wall
tour.where: From the crossing, walk north to the north door, step outside and turn to face the outer north wall.
tour.look: Inside, the north wing has Seti I's raised relief, about 1290 BC: shallow and finely drawn. Outside, his war panorama runs in registers either side of the door. East: his first campaign, nomads on the road to Gaza, chiefs of Lebanon felling cedars. West: Syria, the Libyans, the Hittites. Each half ends with the king smiting prisoners beside lists of conquered places.
tour.story: Find a canal full of crocodiles under a bridge into a fortress: Tjaru, Egypt's north-east border fort. A small figure behind the king's chariot was first carved as an officer called Mehy, then recut as Prince Ramesses, the future Ramesses II. This wall faces north and gets no direct sun in October, so the carving reads evenly all day.
spot: Lebanese chiefs felling cedars
The crocodile canal
The recut figure behind the chariot
tour.ask: Which figure was Mehy, and how can you tell it was recut?

tour.title: The south wing, Ramesses II's wall and the treaty
tour.where: Come back in, cross to the south wing and, if the south door is open, step outside to the outer south wall.
tour.look: Here the reliefs turn to deep sunk relief: Ramesses II finished the hall. Outside, the south wall shows his wars in Palestine and Syria after Kadesh; one fortress is captioned Ashkelon. Look for ghost lines underneath: a first version of the Kadesh battle, plastered over and recarved, half visible again now the plaster has gone.
tour.story: At the east end of this wall, another wall turns south. On its outer face is the Egyptian text of the peace treaty with the Hittites, year 21 of Ramesses II, about 1259 BC: a long block of hieroglyphs, no pictures. The battle scenes beside it are now credited to his son Merenptah. This wall takes full sun: mid-morning or mid-afternoon side light makes the sunk relief read best.
spot: Ghost lines of the first Kadesh version
The treaty text at the corner
tour.ask: Is the treaty corner open today?

tour.title: The two obelisks
tour.where: Walk east along the axis through the ruined Third Pylon to Thutmose I's obelisk, then through the Fourth Pylon to Hatshepsut's, in the narrow hall beyond.
tour.look: Thutmose I's obelisk: about 20 metres of Aswan granite. On each face the central column of text is his; the columns beside it were added by Ramesses IV, some 350 years later. An empty base marks its twin. Hatshepsut's: nearly 30 metres, the tallest standing in Egypt. Around its base are remains of the sandstone masonry that once boxed it in, which is why the lower shaft is so crisp.
tour.story: Hatshepsut (episode l06) removed this hall's roof to raise her pair, and her text says the quarrying took seven months. Her successor Thutmose III later walled them in up to roof height. The usual reading is that he hid her; others note he could have toppled them and did not, and the wall protected them. Her second obelisk fell; its top lies by the Sacred Lake.
spot: Ramesses IV's added text
The sandstone casing at Hatshepsut's base
Her figures cut out, then restored
tour.photo: Stand by Thutmose I's obelisk and fit both in one vertical frame. Morning sun lights their east faces.

tour.title: The sanctuary and the Middle Kingdom court
tour.where: Continue east through the Fifth and Sixth Pylons to two granite pillars, then the dark granite shrine behind them.
tour.look: The pillars carry Thutmose III's heraldic plants: papyrus of the north on the northern one, lotus of the south on the southern. Behind is the red granite barque shrine where the god's boat rested, rebuilt in the name of Philip Arrhidaeus, Alexander the Great's half-brother; on its walls priests carry the boat. Around it, Thutmose III's annals. Behind it, a wide empty court.
tour.story: The annals describe the battle of Megiddo, about 1457 BC, the first battle recorded in detail: Thutmose took the narrow pass his officers feared. The empty court is where Karnak began, Senusret I's limestone temple of around 1950 BC. Only its granite thresholds survived the lime-burners.
spot: Papyrus pillar and lotus pillar
Peg holes that held gold sheeting
Granite thresholds of the first temple
tour.ask: Where is the Megiddo account on these walls?

tour.title: The Festival Hall and the Botanical Garden
tour.where: Cross the empty court to the long building at the east end. The entrance is at its south-west corner.
tour.look: Thutmose III's Akh-menu runs across the main axis. Its columns copy wooden tent poles, wider at the top. On some you can make out painted saints with haloes: the hall later served as a church. Look up for painted ceilings. At the back, a small room with four papyrus columns is the Botanical Garden.
tour.story: The hall was built for the king's jubilee. The Botanical Garden shows plants, birds and animals his campaigns met in Syria and Palestine around year 25 of his reign, laid out like a catalogue. Some are accurate, others fanciful, and botanists still argue over which species are real.
spot: Tent-pole columns
A painted saint
A plant you cannot name
tour.photo: Painted ceiling: phone flat, 1x, no flash.

tour.title: The Sacred Lake and the scarab
tour.where: Leave the Festival Hall to the south and walk to the big rectangular pool. The scarab is at its north-west corner.
tour.look: The lake, about 120 by 77 metres, is fed by groundwater, with stairs down at the edges. At the north-west corner a granite scarab sits on a squat pillar, facing east, towards sunrise. Nearby lies the broken top of Hatshepsut's second obelisk. Looking north-west across the water, the obelisks and the hall line up.
tour.story: Priests washed here before ritual. The beetle is Khepri, the morning sun, rolling the sun like a dung ball. It was made for Amenhotep III's temple on the west bank and moved here later, probably under Taharqa. Walking round it is a modern custom: guides promise luck, a wedding or a return to Egypt.
spot: Khepri facing east
Hatshepsut's fallen obelisk top
Stairs into the lake
tour.photo: The scarab from low down against the sky.

alone.intro: I leave you at the lake for about thirty minutes. Keep one adult with the younger ones and your water in the shade. Use the main axis as a spine: every pylon on it points back west to the exit.

plans.d: Walk round the scarab, then go north to Hatshepsut's obelisk and look at the casing up close. Head west along the axis into the Hypostyle Hall and spend ten slow minutes at the crossing, finding one window grille and one patch of bright paint.

Add the Open Air Museum, entered from the north side of the Great Court, if open; it usually needs its own ticket. Inside: Senusret I's White Chapel, about 1950 BC and crisp as new, and Hatshepsut's quartzite Red Chapel, rebuilt from blocks found in the Third Pylon.

Go straight to the Hypostyle Hall's north wing, which stays in shade. Sit at the foot of a giant column, drink, and play the column game from the kids' list. The Great Court and the lake have almost no shade.

alone.meet: Meet at the foot of Taharqa's column in the Great Court, on the way out, at the time your guide gives. Set an alarm ten minutes early: crossing Karnak takes longer than it looks.

photos.where: Forecourt, on the axis between the two rows of rams.
photos.when: Afternoon, sun behind you. In the morning the gate is backlit.
photos.how: Kneel on the axis, 0.5x, rows leading to the door.
photos.avoid: A black pylon on a white sky in the morning.

photos.where: Beside a ram near the end of a row.
photos.when: Morning: stand on the ram's shady side so nobody squints.
photos.how: Tallest behind, younger ones by the ram's head, phone at chest height.
photos.avoid: The doorway queue and other groups' flags.

photos.where: Foot of the lone column in the Great Court.
photos.when: Before ten or after three, softer light.
photos.how: One line, photographer crouched six metres back, 0.5x vertical.
photos.avoid: The sun right behind the column, which silhouettes you.

photos.where: Hypostyle Hall, nave or northern wing, where sun patches fall.
photos.how: Person in the bright patch, you in the shade; tap their face to expose. Portrait mode works.
photos.avoid: Strangers crossing the patch: wait for a gap.

photos.where: Base of a central column in the Hypostyle Hall.
photos.how: Phone flat on the floor pointing up, 0.5x.
photos.avoid: Flash, which flattens relief and is often not allowed.

photos.where: East side of the Sacred Lake, looking north-west to the obelisks and the hall.
photos.when: Morning, sun behind you in the south-east.
photos.how: Horizontal, water in the bottom third, obelisks on the right third.
photos.avoid: Scaffolding at the edges: crop it.

photos.where: The scarab at the lake's north-west corner.
photos.how: One films 0.5x video while the others circle it, counting aloud.

photos.where: The forecourt, if you come back late or for Sound and Light.
photos.how: Face the pylon, sun behind your right shoulder; family small at the bottom of a wide frame.
photos.avoid: Your own long shadows in the foreground.

details.d: Priests recorded Nile flood heights on the quay about 2,900 to 2,700 years ago. Ask your guide to show you.
High in the First Pylon's doorway, names and dates of nineteenth-century visitors, carved when sand filled the court.
The alabaster block at the foot of Taharqa's column is where the god's boat was set down.
The giant columns are stacks of half-drums. Look for the joints.
Eleven columns in the northern half fell in 1899 and were rebuilt by 1902. Look for cleaner blocks and slight misalignments.
On the south outer wall, a plastered-over Kadesh battle shows under later wars. Best in raking light.
Rows of small holes near the sanctuary held pegs for gold sheeting. The holy core was gilded.
Faded painted saints on the Festival Hall columns, from its time as a church.
The Festival Hall columns swell towards the top, like wooden tent poles.
By the lake, the top of her second obelisk lies on its side: carving made to be seen from thirty metres below, now at eye level.

qa.q: Why was the First Pylon never finished?
qa.a: It is usually dated to Nectanebo I, of the last native dynasty, about 2,350 years ago. The Persians reconquered Egypt in 343 BC, and the later Ptolemies spent their building money on temples such as Edfu and Philae. The ramp shows the work simply stopped.

qa.q: How did they stand a 300-tonne obelisk up?
qa.a: Nobody wrote it down. The unfinished obelisk at Aswan shows the quarrying, with hard dolerite pounders. Barges carried them on the flood; a relief at Hatshepsut's temple shows two obelisks on one boat. For raising, the leading theories are earth and brick ramps, then tipping the stone into a sand-filled pit and letting the sand out slowly.

Probably not as the story is often told. They shared the throne for about twenty years, and attacks on her images began late in his reign, roughly twenty years after her death. The common view today is political: making his son's succession look clean. Walling her obelisks hid them, but he did not topple them.

Several left in antiquity. The Lateran obelisk in Rome, the tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere, was begun at Karnak by Thutmose III and finished by Thutmose IV; the Romans took it in the fourth century AD. The obelisk of Theodosius in Istanbul is another of Thutmose III's from Karnak. The Paris obelisk comes from Luxor Temple.

Mostly not. The inner temple was for priests and the king. People saw the god's boat at festivals and prayed at the outer walls. At the east end of the precinct, Ramesses II built a chapel for the god who hears prayers, where people could bring requests without entering.

From 1903 Georges Legrain dug a court south of the Hypostyle Hall and found a pit packed with statues: about 800 in stone and some 17,000 bronzes. Priests buried them in antiquity, probably in Ptolemaic times, to clear space while keeping sacred objects inside the temple.

qa.q: Is Karnak lined up with the winter solstice?
qa.a: Possibly. The main axis points to about 116 degrees, close to the midwinter sunrise, and the Franco-Egyptian team argues the alignment was deliberate. Other researchers doubt it and point to the river and older buildings. Still debated.

qa.q: What did the priests do all day?
qa.a: Each morning priests purified themselves in the Sacred Lake, opened the shrine, woke the god's statue with hymns, washed, dressed and fed it. The food was then shared among the temple staff. Karnak also ran land, herds and workshops, and employed thousands at its height.

practical: Plan 2 to 2.5 hours: about ninety minutes with me, then thirty alone.
Shade only in the Hypostyle Hall and some side halls. The Great Court and the lake are open sun.
At least a litre of water each. Hats, sunscreen, closed shoes: floors are uneven.
Toilets are normally at the visitor centre by the entrance. Go before you start.
Cruise groups crowd the site from about eight to eleven; the hall thins out around midday.
Guards may offer roped areas or poses for a tip. You may decline; never cross ropes.
The Open Air Museum usually needs its own ticket: check on the day.
Sound and Light is optional in your programme, in French. The boat sails to Esna on Day 5, so check which evening it fits.

kids.d: Count the rams that still have a king between their paws, one row each. Closest guess wins the first seat on the coach.
Hold hands and see how many of you it takes to circle a giant column. Then work out how many of your tallest family member, stacked, reach the top at 21 metres.
Find raised relief in the north half of the hall and sunk relief in the south half. Explain the difference without touching the wall.
In the Botanical Garden, draw one plant or bird. At dinner, the others guess what it is.
Teenagers: did Thutmose III wall in Hatshepsut's obelisk to hide her or to keep it? One minute per side.

glossary.d: King of the gods, the hidden one, fused with the sun. Karnak is his house.
A monumental gate of two sloping towers.
A hall whose roof rests on columns.
High windows above a lower roof that light the middle of a hall.
Thutmose III's Festival Hall, 'Splendid of Monuments'.
Small blocks from Akhenaten's buildings, reused as fill.
The morning sun as a scarab beetle.

tonight: If you could take one object home from Karnak, which one?
Thutmose III or Hatshepsut: who comes out better from what we saw?
Ramesses II carved his name on other kings' work. Stealing or recycling?

sites.name: Edfu, the Temple of Horus
sites.kicker: Day 6 morning · by horse carriage from the boat
sites.hook: The best-preserved temple in Egypt, and the clearest textbook of how a temple works.

story.title: Hathor comes to visit
story.text: Every year, in high summer, a statue of the goddess Hathor was lifted onto a boat at her temple at Dendera, north of Luxor, and carried upriver to Edfu, a journey of days. There she met the god Horus, and they were married again in a festival called the Beautiful Meeting. Crowds lined the river and the temple walls carry the stories. The temple itself was buried in sand and houses until the 1860s, when it was dug out. Because of that, it is nearly complete.

steps: Horse-carriage ride from the quay to the temple
The granite falcons and the great pylon
The open court with columns on three sides
The first hall of columns (hypostyle)
Second hall, the offering hall, the sanctuary
The sanctuary: the granite shrine
The walkway round the outside: Horus against Set (ask)

dont_miss.d: A granite falcon in a crown stands at the gate. The god protecting the entrance.
A giant king grabbing his enemies by the hair. It is a symbolic picture, repeated on every pylon, and it keeps order.
As you walk inwards, the floor rises, the ceiling lowers and the light fades. That is by design.
In the sanctuary a polished stone shrine is much older than the temple. It was reused from the earlier building.

dont_miss.t: The walls are full of text
dont_miss.d: Edfu has more hieroglyphic text than almost any other temple: festival rules, building records, a list of the temple library.

easy: Look at the faces on the reliefs: many have been chiselled off by early Christians, who lived in and around the temple.
The ceilings in some halls are black from old cooking fires.
Look for the tall grooves in the pylon. Flagpoles with banners were set in them.
Small rooms off the main halls were storerooms, a treasury and even a 'library' of papyrus scrolls.
The Ptolemies were Greek kings. Notice how they dress as pharaohs on the walls.
ask: How do we read the sequence of rooms, and where would the priests have walked?
Why were the Ptolemies, who were Greek, building a temple in this style?
Can we see the walkway around the outside with the scenes of Horus and Set?
How did the temple stay so complete?
What is the Beautiful Meeting?
quests: Look closer
Find a scene where the king gives something to a god. What is he holding, and what is the god holding?
Estimate
The pylon is about 36 m high. If a floor is 3 m, how many floors? Compare it with a building near home.
tips: The carriage ride is part of the experience. A small tip for the driver is normal. Ask the guide what is usual.
Early morning is quieter. The stone is cool and the light enters the court from the side.
Temple interiors are dim. Phone torches are handy, but do not shine them on painted ceilings.

sites.name: Kom Ombo
sites.kicker: Day 6 afternoon · on a bend of the river
sites.hook: A temple with twin doors: one half for a crocodile god and one half for a falcon god.
facts: from about 180 BC, under the Ptolemies

story.title: Two gods, one roof
story.text: Most temples serve one god. This one has two of everything: two entrances, two halls, two sanctuaries, side by side. The northern half belongs to Haroeris, a form of the falcon god Horus, and the southern half to Sobek, the crocodile god of the river. The temple sits on a bend of the Nile where sandbanks were once covered in basking crocodiles. Sobek was feared and honoured. Mummified crocodiles were left here as offerings.

steps: Arrive at the temple on its bluff above the river
The courtyard and the double entrance
The two halls of columns
The two sanctuaries at the back
The walls on the outside: the medical instruments
The Crocodile Museum, if included (ask)

dont_miss.d: North and south halves mirror each other. Walk both and compare.
A man with a crocodile's head, receiving offerings. Look for the crocodile on a shrine.
A relief on the outer wall shows what look like medical tools: a lancet, a sponge, forceps. Historians are careful about what exactly it shows.
Texts on the wall list the festivals of the year.
The temple is placed to catch the river bend. Turn round and look at the Nile.

easy: Look for a round stone well with a stair: it is the Nilometer, used to measure the flood.
Crocodile mummies of all sizes were found nearby. The Crocodile Museum next door shows some.
The columns have capitals shaped like papyrus and lotus. Notice how the colours remain on a few.
A small chapel of Hathor was used to store crocodile mummies.
ask: Why two gods in one temple?
How do we know which half is which?
What does the medical relief really show?
How did people look after and mummify crocodiles?
Did Sobek protect people from crocodiles or did people fear him?
quests: Look closer
Find a mirrored pair of scenes, one on each side of the temple. What small differences can you spot?
Debate
A crocodile god and a falcon god sharing a temple: who is likely to have been more popular with farmers, and why?
tips: A short stop at a lovely time of day. The temple can be crowded by cruise groups, so move along the walls.
The Crocodile Museum is a separate building. Your programme does not list it, so ask.

sites.name: Aswan: High Dam, felucca and Elephantine
sites.hook: The place where the Nile was stopped, and one of the loveliest river views in Egypt.
facts: High Dam about 45 min, felucca about 1 h
built 1960 to 1970, about 3.8 km long, 111 m high

story.title: The lake that moved two temples
story.text: For thousands of years, the Nile rose every summer and fell every autumn. In 1970, the High Dam ended that. It stored the water in a lake nearly 500 km long, gave Egypt power and protected it against drought and flood. But the lake covered Nubia, a region with its own language, villages and temples. Around 100,000 people were moved and a worldwide appeal helped to save the temples, including Philae and Abu Simbel. You will see one of them tomorrow.

steps: High Dam: a viewpoint over the lake and the dam wall
The Lotus monument beside the dam
Philae temple (next page)
Felucca on the Nile around Elephantine
Elephantine: look for the Nilometer and old town

dont_miss.d: Three kilometres of rock and earth. On one side, a lake. On the other, the old river.
A wooden sailing boat with a triangle sail. The captain uses wind and current, as people have here for thousands of years.
Named 'elephant' either from the ivory trade or from the shape of the granite boulders in the river.
Dark granite boulders in the river mark the First Cataract, the old southern border of Egypt.

easy: Granite here is the stone of obelisks. Look at the pink and black rocks on the shore.
The Nubian houses on the west bank are painted in bright colours.
Look for the Nilometer steps on Elephantine, used to measure the river's height.
Birdwatchers love this stretch. Look for egrets on the rocks.
ask: What did the dam give Egypt, and what did it take away?
Where did the Nubians go, and what do they say about it today?
How did the flood work before the dam?
What does the captain do to sail against the wind?
quests: Look closer
Find rock that is not sandstone. What colour is it? Where have you seen it earlier in the trip?
Estimate
The dam is about 3.8 km long. How long would it take to walk across at a normal pace?
tips: On the felucca, sit as the captain asks. Sunscreen and a hat are needed because there is no shade.
Swimming from the boat is not recommended. Keep phones on lanyards or in bags.

sites.name: Philae, the temple that moved
sites.kicker: Day 7 morning · by motorboat to Agilkia Island
sites.hook: The sanctuary of Isis, dismantled block by block and rebuilt on higher ground in the 1970s.
facts: from about 380 BC to Roman times

story.title: The last hieroglyphs
story.text: Philae was the last of Egypt's temples to close. While Rome became Christian, pilgrims kept coming here to honour Isis, the mother goddess. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription we know of, from 24 August AD 394, is carved here. The temple was closed in the sixth century. Fifteen centuries later, the rising waters behind the dams threatened it again. Engineers built a wall around the island, pumped it dry, cut the temples into blocks, numbered them and rebuilt them on a neighbouring island that was shaped to look like the original.

steps: Motorboat ride from the landing to the island
The Kiosk of Nectanebo and the west colonnade
The First Pylon with the giant king figures
The court and the Birth House (Mammisi)
The Second Pylon and the hall
The inner sanctuary of Isis
The Gate of Hadrian and the Osiris rooms
Trajan's Kiosk by the water, the last view

dont_miss.d: The temple rises from the water. This is the view travellers painted in the nineteenth century.
Huge figures of a king smiting enemies in front of gods. The figures are scratched with early Christian crosses.
The last hieroglyphic inscription is nearby. Ask the guide where, and for the relief of the god of the Nile in his cave.
A Roman kiosk by the water, never finished. It is on every postcard.
Ask whether any building marks from the 1970s relocation are visible on the stones.

easy: Look closely at the reliefs on the pylons: some have Christian crosses carved on them.
The Birth House walls show Isis nursing the baby Horus.
Graffiti from 1799: French soldiers of Napoleon's expedition left an inscription at Philae. Ask the guide.
Look for the Nilometer at the foot of the island.
Agilkia Island was reshaped to resemble the original Philae. The old island is now under the lake.
ask: Who was Isis, and why did her worship spread to Rome?
Where is the old Philae island today?
How were the blocks numbered and moved?
What did the temple look like in colour?
Where is the French inscription from 1799?
quests: Look closer
Find a Christian cross carved on a temple wall. What does it tell you about how the temple was used after its gods left?
Estimate
Tens of thousands of blocks were moved. Say 40,000. If a crew moved 20 per day, how long would the job take? What would you want on your crew?
tips: Boats are small and the sun is bright. Hat, sunscreen, water.
The Sound and Light show at Philae is optional (65 EUR per person, in French, as listed in your programme).
Stone steps can be uneven. Watch your footing on the quay.

sites.name: Abu Simbel (optional)
sites.hook: Four colossal statues of Ramesses II carved into a cliff, 280 km south of Aswan.
facts: By coach, 130 EUR per person (programme price)
By plane, 415 EUR per person (programme price)

story.title: The sun that visits twice a year
story.text: Ramesses II had a temple cut into the cliff so that on two days in the year the rising sun reaches deep inside and lights the statues in the sanctuary. The dates are about 22 February and 22 October. After the temple was cut into blocks in the 1960s and moved to higher ground, the dates shifted by a day. Your Day 8 is 28 October, so you will not see it. You will still see four seated colossi, each about 20 m high, and a smaller temple for his queen Nefertari.

steps: Early start (by coach, the road convoy leaves in the dark)
The facade of the Great Temple
Inside: the pillared hall and the sanctuary
The Small Temple of Nefertari and Hathor
A look at how the temples were moved

dont_miss.d: Four seated colossi of Ramesses II. Count the small figures at their feet: they are his family.
Statues of the king as Osiris line the hall. The walls show the Battle of Kadesh.
One of the rare temples where a queen is shown at the same size as the king.
Behind the facade, the hill is man-made. It is a concrete dome that holds the relocated temple.
